title: Aliases: fine to type, wrong to ship
summary: Read the shortcuts everyone types (gci, ?, %, select), know why they break scripts across machines, and let PSScriptAnalyzer spell them out.

steps.title: What an alias is
body: An **alias** is a short second name for a command. They save typing at the prompt, and you will see them in every
answer on the internet:
| Alias | Command | | Alias | Command |
| `gci`, `dir` | `Get-ChildItem` | | `?`, `where` | `Where-Object` |
| `%`, `foreach` | `ForEach-Object` | | `select` | `Select-Object` |
| `gm` | `Get-Member` | | `cd`, `sl` | `Set-Location` |
| `iwr` | `Invoke-WebRequest` | | `irm` | `Invoke-RestMethod` |
`Get-Alias gci` tells you what an alias means; `Get-Alias -Definition Get-ChildItem` lists the aliases of a command.
**The catch: aliases are not the same everywhere.** To make Windows users feel at home, PowerShell on Windows maps
`ls`, `cat`, `sort`, `cp`, `rm`, `ps` and friends to cmdlets. **On Linux and macOS those aliases do not exist**: `ls`
and `sort` run the real GNU tools, which know nothing about objects. And Windows PowerShell 5.1 had `curl` and `wget`
as aliases of `Invoke-WebRequest`, so `curl -X POST ...` from a tutorial failed with a confusing parameter error;
PowerShell 7 removed them, so `curl` is the real curl.exe that ships with Windows.

steps.prompt: A script that works on your Windows laptop fails on the Linux build agent (with PowerShell 7) with `sort: cannot read: Length: No such file or directory`. The line is `Get-ChildItem ./out | sort Length`. Why?
options: On Linux `sort` is not an alias of `Sort-Object`, so the GNU `sort` program ran and took `Length` as a file name
The build agent has an older PowerShell
steps.explain: PowerShell looks up aliases before programs on the PATH. On Windows `sort` is an alias; on Linux there is no such alias, so `/usr/bin/sort` runs. Spelling out `Sort-Object` works on both.

steps.title: Why scripts spell everything out
body: At the prompt, type whatever is fastest. In a **script**, a teammate or a scheduler will run it on another machine and
someone will read it in a review. So scripts use:
- **full command names**: `Where-Object`, not `?`;
- **full parameter names**: `-Descending`, not `-desc` or `-d`. An abbreviation works only while it is unique; the next
version of a command can add a parameter with the same prefix and the script breaks;
- **named parameters** rather than positions where it helps the reader: `Copy-Item -Path $a -Destination $b`.
You do not have to type the long names: **Tab** completes commands, parameters and even property names.
PSScriptAnalyzer finds aliases for you (`PSAvoidUsingCmdletAliases`), and `-Fix` rewrites them in place:
```powershell
Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path ./report.ps1 -IncludeRule PSAvoidUsingCmdletAliases
Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path ./report.ps1 -Fix       # rewrites the file: review the diff before committing
In VS Code the PowerShell extension runs the same analyzer as you type, and Shift+Alt+F (Format Document) can
expand aliases too.

steps.title: Spell out a pasted one-liner
prompt: `~/scripts/report-logs.ps1` is a one-liner someone pasted from their prompt into a script that now runs on Linux
agents. Run it, then make it production-ready:
3. the output stays exactly the same.

checks.name: same output as before
checks.fail: The script should still print the four logs over 2 KB with their sizes, biggest first.

hints: `Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer ~/scripts/report-logs.ps1` lists each alias and what it stands for.
`Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer ~/scripts/report-logs.ps1 -Fix` replaces the aliases in the file. It does not touch abbreviated parameters.
steps.explain: Run the analyzer in CI, not only in your editor: `Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path . -Recurse -Severity Warning, Error -EnableExit` fails the build when it finds something. Module 5 sets that up for a real module.

steps.prompt: At the prompt, or in a script that others run?
buckets: Spell it out in a script
steps.explain: Both columns do the same thing on Windows. Only the right-hand column does the same thing on every machine and reads well in a review.

steps.prompt: In Windows PowerShell 5.1, `curl -X POST https://api.example.com/hooks` fails with `A parameter cannot be found that matches parameter name 'X'`. In PowerShell 7 the same line works. Why?
options: In 5.1 `curl` is an alias of `Invoke-WebRequest`, which has no `-X`; PowerShell 7 removed that alias, so curl.exe runs
PowerShell 7 added a `-X` parameter to Invoke-WebRequest
steps.explain: Use `curl.exe` explicitly in 5.1, or better, `Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post`, which returns objects instead of text (module 6).
